title: At Which Transformer Layer Do Jailbreak Signals Become Detectable?

original_idea.problem: The specific layer at which jailbreak-vs-benign separation becomes reliable has not been ablated across model sizes.
original_idea.direction: Extract residual stream activations at every 4th layer. Train and evaluate a linear probe at each layer. Plot AUROC vs. layer depth.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Finding the earliest detection layer enables real-time, low-latency jailbreak interception. Detecting at layer 8 vs 28 dramatically changes inference cost.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: earliest detection layer -> low-latency interception -> cost reduction for production safety systems. Directly actionable for system-level safety architecture.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires activation extraction at multiple layers and training linear probes at each. Intermediate complexity but the methodology is systematic and repeatable. Beginners need guidance on hooks.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: single AUROC-vs-layer plot. Systematic procedure: extract at each layer, train probe, evaluate. Obvious deliverable. Well-defined success criteria.

novelty.reasoning: This question is now substantially addressed by multiple papers. 'Do Internal Layers of LLMs Reveal Patterns for Jailbreak Detection?' (arXiv:2510.06594, NeurIPS 2025 Workshop) directly analyzes layer-wise jailbreak detection patterns, finding that MHA representations outperform layer outputs and optimal layers correspond to roughly 14-25% of network depth. 'What Features in Prompts Jailbreak LLMs?' (BlackboxNLP 2025) trains single-layer probes and evaluates across layers. The Chain-of-Thought Hijacking paper identifies mid vs. late layer roles in safety. ALERT (2026) uses layer-wise amplification. The AUROC-vs-layer experiment is the core contribution of existing work, leaving little room for novelty.
